exemplars.name: HashMap internals
exemplars.question: How does HashMap work internally in Java?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand hashing, collision resolution, and the Java 8 treeification upgrade — not just the API surface
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'it's just a key-value store backed by an array' without explaining how hashCode maps to a bucket or how collisions are resolved
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java 8 upgrade from linked-list chains to red-black trees at TREEIFY_THRESHOLD=8, explain load factor math, and describe the pre-sizing pattern for production maps

sections.title: One-Sentence Mental Model
sections.content: HashMap is a Node<K,V>[] array where the slot index is derived from the key's hashCode, and conflicts in the same slot are resolved first by chaining (linked list) then by treeifying (red-black tree) once the chain grows long enough.

sections.title: Step 1 — Computing the bucket index
Step 2 — Collision resolution: chains and trees
sections.content:
When two keys land in the same bucket:

- **Java 7 and earlier** — a singly-linked list grows at the head of the bucket. Worst-case lookup is O(n) if all keys hash to the same bucket — a real DoS vector.
- **Java 8+** — once a bucket's chain exceeds `TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8` nodes, the chain converts to a **red-black tree**, capping worst-case lookup at O(log n). If the tree shrinks below `UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6`, it reverts to a linked list to save memory.

A `null` key is always assigned to bucket 0.

sections.title: Step 3 — Resize and rehash
hashCode + equals contract and frequency-count pattern
Key Points
sections.content:
- HashMap is a **Node[] bucket array** — the index is computed by `(capacity - 1) & hash(key)`, where `hash()` XOR-spreads the upper 16 bits of `hashCode()` into the lower 16 for better distribution
- Collisions form a **linked list** that upgrades to a **red-black tree** after 8 entries (Java 8+). Worst-case goes from O(n) to O(log n) — this was added to prevent hash-flooding DoS attacks
- Default capacity is **16**, load factor **0.75** — resize triggers at just 12 entries. Pre-size with `new HashMap<>(1024)` when you know the volume to avoid O(n) rehashing spikes
- The **equals/hashCode contract**: if `a.equals(b)` then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true. Java `record` types handle this automatically; manual classes that break it silently lose entries
- HashMap allows **one null key** (bucket 0) and null values. `ConcurrentHashMap` allows neither — a common follow-up question

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HashMap is essentially a **bucket array** — a `Node[]` where each slot is indexed by the key's hash. When you call `map.put("name", "John")`, Java takes `"name".hashCode()`, spreads the bits using XOR to reduce clustering, and then masks with `capacity - 1` to get a bucket index. Because capacity is always a power of two, that mask works as a fast modulo. That's why `put` and `get` are O(1) on average.

The interesting part is **collision handling**. Say `"Aa"` and `"BB"` have the same hashCode in Java — they'd land in the same bucket. Before Java 8, this formed a linked list, and worst-case was O(n). Attackers actually exploited this for DoS attacks. **Java 8 introduced treeification**: once a chain exceeds 8 nodes, it converts to a red-black tree, capping worst-case at O(log n). Below 6 nodes it reverts to save overhead.

The production gotcha is **resizing**. Default capacity is 16, load factor 0.75, so resize hits at just 12 entries — it doubles the array and rehashes everything. I've seen this cause p99 latency spikes in hot paths. The fix is simple: `new HashMap<>(2048)` if you expect ~1000 entries.

The **equals/hashCode contract** is the classic interview follow-up. Here's a concrete example: if you have a class `Person` where you override `equals()` to compare by name, but forget `hashCode()`, then `map.put(new Person("Alice"), "data")` and `map.get(new Person("Alice"))` return `null` — the two Person objects are equal but the map looks in different buckets. Java `record` types generate both automatically, which is one reason I prefer them for map keys.

One more thing: HashMap allows one `null` key — it always goes to bucket 0. `ConcurrentHashMap` allows neither null keys nor null values, which is a very common follow-up.
